articles.title: Su-30MKI May Get Meteor BVR Missiles After Tejas Mk1A Integration
articles.text:
With HAL confirming that the second batch of Tejas Mk1A jets that are to come with the Uttam Aesa Fire Control Radar over the Israeli-supplied ELM-2052 Aesa Radar, MBDA, has given green signals for the second batch of Tejas Mk1A to come integrated with the MBDA-developed Meteor. Very long BVR missiles, breaking away from being only exclusive with the Rafale fleet, IAF is showing keen interest in the missile also being adopted into another jet after the Tejas Mk1A programme. If approved, IAF could see Meteor BVR missiles also on the upgraded Su-30MKI jets that are to come with locally developed Virupaksha Aesa Radar.
Virupaksha Aesa Radar is just an evolved variant of the baseline Uttam Aesa Fire Control Radar that will have over twice the TrMs in it than what will go into the Tejas Mk1A, but most of the software will remain the same, including some of the backend processing system that will allow the radar to be integrated into the aircraft if approved.
In 2019 MBDA refused integration on the Tejas Mk1A and told the IAF that the Mirage 2000 and Su-30MKI were “not suitable” for the missile. The stated reason was that European governments holding MBDA shares had barred integration of Meteor on non-European fire-control radars to protect the missile’s encrypted data link and guidance technology.
MBDA indicated it would reconsider if the aircraft carried DRDO’s indigenous Uttam AESA rather than the Israeli EL/M-2052. Virupaksha satisfies the condition of the MBDA set by the MBDA, and the Uttam Aesa radar planned for the Tejas Mk1A and MkII and even for the AMCA Program will all share the same hardware with different antenna configurations and TRM technology between GaS and GaN, but most of the weapons that are to be integrated into the radar for the guidance will allow one missile to be added to one platform to integrate it into another jet with a similar radar type, which is much easier for the planners.
Meteor needs a two-way data link and mid-course updates, which means deep integration with the aircraft’s fire control and access to source code. MBDA cited high integration cost and radar mismatch when the Mirage 2000 upgrade was proposed, but with India now willing to pay for the missile to be part of the Tejas Mk1A arsenal, it is likely that MBDA will allow it to be part of the MKI that will have locally developed the Virupaksha Aesa Radar.
Astra Mk2 has completed integration on the Su-30MKI, including captive carriage and systems compatibility trials, with a validated 240 km range and induction expected around end-2026; Astra Mk3, at a projected 350 km, is targeted for 2028–29. Meteor on the Super Sukhoi could be seen as another missile rather than the main BVR for the type even if MBDA clears the deal.
RAUNAK KUNDE

articles.title: AI relief fails to lift legacy IT stocks as earnings worries weigh
articles.text: Mumbai: Has Indian IT turned the corner?After surging more than 17% in October, the Nifty IT index appears to have lost momentum, declining nearly 2% so far in November, although the Sensex and Nifty harnessed new-found enthusiasm from foreign funds to climb more than 10% in the run-up to Diwali and its immediate aftermath.Legacy IT stocks have stagnated despite a precipitous plunge in AI-heavy bets across Asia, putting a question mark over whether earnings concerns at outsourcing firms would continue to keep prices - and valuation multiples - in restraint despite obvious opportunities arising from a sectoral churn.135820397Since the beginning of October, South Korea's Kospi and Taiwan's stock index have fallen around 20% and 13%, respectively. Japan's Nikkei has declined 10%, while the Nasdaq Composite has lost 6%. The Shanghai Composite and Hang Seng have fallen 4.4% and 2.4%, respectively, reflecting the correction in global AI-related stocks.The September-quarter earnings of Indian IT companies, meanwhile, point to an uneven recovery, with mid-tier players outperforming larger peers while underlying demand conditions remain largely unchanged. Choice Institutional Equities said companies under its coverage reported average sequential revenue growth of around 5.4% for tier-2 players, compared with nearly 1.1% for tier-1 companies.Read more: BSE launches 14 new sector indices, expands BSE 500-based suite to 20 benchmarksCoforge led the mid-tier pack with 10.9% growth, followed by Persistent Systems at 7.8%, while Tech Mahindra and HCLTech led among larger companies.However, healthy deal bookings have yet to translate into commensurate revenue growth. Phased transitions, staggered project ramp-ups and longer client decision-making cycles continue to delay revenue conversion.Shorter-cycle AI engagements, typically lasting one to two quarters, are also limiting the visibility traditionally associated with large, multi-year deals, Choice said.A key concern for the sector is the changing economics of technology services as clients increasingly use AI to improve productivity and reduce costs. While AI is creating new business opportunities, these gains are yet to fully offset pricing pressure in traditional services.Kotak Institutional Equities estimates gross deflation of around 7% and net deflation of 3.5% for companies as clients seek a greater share of productivity savings through contract renewals.Read more: 12 bluechip stocks within 5% of their 52-week highs; should you chase them now?Sandeep Gogia, MD and co-head, Investment Banking, Equirus Capital, said pressure on enterprise clients to improve returns on AI-related investments, alongside concerns around safety, security and token-cost optimisation, could create fresh opportunities for IT services providers. "Integration of systems of records and data systems with systems of intelligence and AI models is not plug and play," Gogia said, pointing to opportunities in data engineering, application modernisation, cloud migration and cybersecurity as enterprises move towards large-scale AI implementation.On profitability, Choice said operational efficiency and cost discipline had partly offset wage and delivery-related pressures, although margin performance remained mixed. Kotak expects margins at large IT companies to remain largely stable, with rupee depreciation providing some support. However, pricing pressure and AI-related investments could weigh on profitability.The earnings outlook also remains uneven. Kotak expects Infosys to lower its FY27 revenue growth guidance to 1.5-2.5%.

articles.title: Airlines issue advisories amid FAA ground stop
articles.text: Airlines including Air Canada and American Airlines issued passenger advisories after a nationwide ground stop imposed by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) disrupted flight operations across the United States, triggering cancellations and departure delays.Air Canada cancelled all flights to and from the US for the remainder of the evening, warning that services between Canada, the Caribbean and South America that transit US airspace could also be affected.Also Read: US flights remain suspended after nationwide FAA ground stop over communication outageAmerican Airlines said some flights at select airports had begun receiving clearance to depart, although most departures remained paused. The carrier warned of continued schedule disruptions and unavoidable cancellations, urging passengers to check their flight status and travel alerts for updates.San Francisco International Airport (SFO) also issued an update, confirming that Pacific-bound flights, including services to Hawaii and Asia, had been cleared to depart from the airport. It advised passengers to check directly with their airlines for the latest information.&mdash; aircanada (@aircanada) The nationwide ground stop was lifted at 8:15 pm ET, according to Reuters.Why did the FAA impose a nationwide ground stop?The FAA grounded flights nationwide on Friday afternoon following communications problems at regional air traffic control centres, citing extraordinary circumstances and safety concerns.Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the outage affected 22 regional centres responsible for directing aircraft travelling between airports across the country. FAA technicians were investigating the problem.Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication that the disruption was the result of a deliberate attack, describing it as a telecommunications outage.&mdash; americanair (@americanair) The incident marked the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when a malfunction in a key FAA computer system disrupted air travel. The previous such shutdown had followed the September 11, 2001, attacks.Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said the outage appeared similar to a communications failure at a regional air traffic control centre in September, which disrupted hundreds of flights across the Northeast, but on a nationwide scale.

articles.title: Starship flight 15 powers to orbit—setting up a possible catch on Saturday
articles.text:
STARBASE, Texas—Starship lifted off right on schedule Friday from South Texas, making its 15th test flight in more than three years.

The largely successful launch took place in the early evening; as the massive rocket rose into the atmosphere, the Sun sank toward the western horizon. Conditions were ideal for the launch, with the atmospheric winds so calm the rocket’s white plume did not dissipate for many minutes. The weather in South Texas is not always comfortable; summers are long and hot. Friday evening was perfect at Starbase.

The first stage ascended toward space flawlessly, releasing the upper stage above the Gulf of Mexico. From there, the Starship upper stage ignited its Raptor engines and powered its way into a nominal orbit. This was the second time SpaceX has flown Starship into low-Earth orbit.

articles.title: FAA orders third nationwide ground stop in its history
articles.text:
On Friday afternoon, days after expanding use of an AI tool, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop, halting departures from all US airports. Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy announced the ground stop on X, citing a "communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers." Duffy promised updates as more information is known and said FAA staff were troubleshooting the problem.

Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said that the ground stop was not prompted by a security threat. "This is a telecommunications outage out of the FAA. Out of an abundance of caution, we have grounded all of the flights," Mullin said. "There's no indication as of yet that this is a nefarious attack against us."

Mullin said the FAA would handle incoming international flights on a case-by-case basis.

The stop was finally lifted around 8:30 PM Eastern Time, but only after thousands of flights were canceled or delayed, leaving travelers stranded. The FAA has not yet confirmed a reason for the stop.

Original story below:

"The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers," said US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy in a statement. "FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them."

A spokesperson at the FAA press office reached by phone said he was unable to provide further information. And an email response from the agency repeated Duffy's statement.

The FAA ATCSCC advisory halts departing flights and says international flights will be dealt with individually.

The notice says, "Due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety. Attention all aircraft operators, by order of the Federal Aviation Command Center all airports are ground stopped. All departing traffic should remain stopped until further notice. Inbound international flights will be managed on a case by case basis."

Doug Yakel, public information officer for San Francisco International Airport, said, "FAA confirms nationwide ground stop, other reporting indicates a communications issue between Air Route Traffic Control Centers (ARTCCs). Aircraft already enroute to SFO still landing here but departing aircraft not taking off right now."

An update issued at 2:02 pm PT described the problem as "a temporary telecommunications outage."

The FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure (FTI) is managed by L3Harris. The network provides secure communication between more than 4,400 facilities.

The grounding follows on the heels of a major Microsoft outage that has affected many Microsoft-hosted services, particularly email, for more than 24 hours so far. There's no indication presently that the two incidents are related.

We'll update this story as more information becomes available.®

Updated at 0211 Saturday UTC to reflect the lifting of the ground stop.

Updated to add at 2353 UTC

CBS News reports that “an update to the private communications network that connects America’s air traffic control system caused the system to reboot. When the FAA’s telecommunication infrastructure rebooted, it crashed, causing the communications outage. The system is operated by L3Harris.”

L3Harris has not responded to a request for comment.

Updated to add at 2340 UTC

Air Space Intelligence (ASI), awarded the FAA’s $875 million, 12-year contract for its new Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (SMART) system, has issued a statement asserting that its products played no role in the FAA’s flight suspension. “The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said.

articles.title: Millions of Americans are not taking their GLP-1 drugs as prescribed
articles.text:
GLP-1 medications are everywhere these days. The peptide-based drugs are both highly effective and wildly popular for diabetes, weight loss and a growing range of connected chronic health conditions, including cardiovascular disease and obstructive sleep apnea. But, amid the boom, the latest data suggests millions of Americans have turned to unapproved versions and are using the potent drugs in ways doctors never intended, raising questions about what that real-world use means for safety and efficacy.

In a study published this week, researchers at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention broke down survey data of GLP-1 use collected between July and August of 2025. Based on responses from over 8,000 US adults, the researchers estimate that about one in 10 US adults (9.8 percent) used a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist, aka GLP-1 medication, in 2025. That's around 27 million adults. The study was published in the CDC's Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report.

Among GLP-1 users, nearly half (44 percent) reported using their GLP-1 in a way that was different from how it was prescribed. Users skipped doses, delayed getting refills, and used smaller doses than prescribed, among other changes. More than half of the people modifying how they used the drug said the changes were because of cost or availability reasons. Cost and access barriers were most pronounced among younger GLP-1 users. Fifty-eight percent of adults 14­–39 years old who modified their use cited cost as a barrier, compared with just 20 percent of adults 65 or older who said the same.

articles.title: Chinese AI labs are training models on Nvidia's Blackwell despite export controls, says ex-OpenAI engineer
articles.text:
US export controls are not stopping AI labs in China from using restricted Nvidia chips, according to a report from a former OpenAI engineer.

Will DePue, who left the AI giant earlier this year to launch Unemployment Labs, an AI research consultancy, published forensic evidence showing that "DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group have gained access to Nvidia's Blackwell GPUs, despite restrictions on exporting these chips to China, and are using that hardware to create their AI models."

"This sounds insane, but I discovered that almost every AI model carries a hidden signature of the GPU that trained it," said DePue in a social media post. "When a model is first set up, the starting values of its weights are laid out in a pattern that depends on the exact GPU. Each combination of GPU and seed number produces a unique pattern – a sort of fingerprint of the hardware used to create the model. Traces of that pattern survive training into the published model."

It doesn't sound that insane. The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang followed from revelations that he had an affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who, in 2023, founded Singapore-based Megaspeed International. That company is reportedly under investigation by US authorities for allegedly smuggling Nvidia chips to China.

Huang's departure coincides with a renewed push to tighten US chip export controls. House Speaker Mike Johnson supports the idea. And there are at least four bills awaiting consideration that aim to limit China's access to leading edge AI tech: the AI Overwatch Act, the Chip Security Act, Match Act, and the Cloud Security Act.

On Monday, US Senators Jim Banks (R-Ind.) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) cited Jensen Huang's "relationship with a suspected Chinese spy" as a justification for passing the AI Overwatch Act, which would codify the Trump administration's existing chip export controls. The Trump administration on Thursday said it's not sure whether Alice Huang was a spy, an allegation denied by Beijing and currently under investigation by the FBI.

Whatever the case, the current rules clearly are not working. Only a few weeks ago, Lava, an Israel-based security company, said it had found "32 Nvidia B300 GPUs, part of Nvidia's Blackwell Ultra generation, through publicly exposed monitoring endpoints with IP addresses geolocated to China."

These GPUs, Lava noted, are subject to US export controls [PDF]. The security biz said its findings followed from the exposure of monitoring systems intended for internal infrastructure management that were publicly exposed.

How DePue reached his conclusion

The analysis published through DePue's consultancy, "Top Chinese Frontier AI Models Carry the Fingerprint of Export-Controlled Nvidia Blackwell GPUs," takes a different approach: analyzing the published weights of various models from Chinese AI labs.

As described in the report, model weights – the parameters that change in relation to training data – must be initialized with some value. One method for doing so involves a pseudorandom number generation (PRNG) algorithm called Philox. The algorithm starts with a seed value that produces the same set of initial values whenever it's run.

Using PyTorch, initialization can be done by creating multiple GPU threads that work in parallel, with the help of Nvidia's cuRAND library. And because this process is not truly random, it's possible to select a chip and a seed value, generate the initial weights for that hardware and compare that pattern to a model's published weights.

"I searched more than six trillion combinations of chip layout and seed number and matched them to open-weights models," said DePue. "In doing so, I found conclusive evidence that six Chinese AI models – including DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3, and MiniMax-M3 – were initialized on Nvidia Blackwell systems. Four of the models match Grace Blackwell, the GB200 and GB300 parts in Nvidia's flagship liquid-cooled rack-scale systems."

Noting that this is the first time MiniMax and Ant Group have been publicly linked to usage of Nvidia's Blackwell, he also cited several limitations to his approach. One is that usage of Blackwell GPUs doesn't prove where the GPUs were located, so it's possible some of these Chinese labs used this hardware through US providers – a loophole the Cloud Security Act aims to close.

DePue's report includes initial seed values that linked DeepSeek-V3 to Nvidia's Hopper and DeepSeek-V4-Flash to Blackwell, for those who wish to attempt to reproduce the results. DuPue claims that multiple senior researchers, both independent and inside frontier AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic, have confirmed the result.

Coincidentally, OpenAI and Anthropic have each complained about Chinese labs copying their models through distillation, a pastime also noted by the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. ®

articles.title: This year’s bug count just passed 100K
articles.text:
Chalk up a new record for vulns. The number of Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) found and disclosed so far in 2026 surpassed 100,000 on Friday - more than double 2025’s total - and the reason can be summed up in two letters: AI.

“It’s kind of wild,” Josh Bressers, VulnCheck’s director of coordinated vulnerability disclosure, told The Register. “The thing that almost scares the bejesus out of me is while 100K sounds like a lot, in a couple years we're going to say, remember when it was only 100K?”

As of the time of our interview, about 4 pm UTC on Friday, VulnCheck counted 100,222 CVEs, he said. Microsoft alone added 1,094 security flaws to the total count on Tuesday, following 1,474 vulnerabilities the month before.

“There's no denying the fact that vulnerability hunting with AI is driving a majority of what we're seeing.” All the major CVE Numbering Authorities (CNAs) - these are the organizations authorized by the CVE program to assign unique identifiers to security vulnerabilities - like VulnCheck, Microsoft, Oracle, GitHub, and other large enterprise IT vendors “are just screaming into the atmosphere right now,” Bressers said. “It’s AI.”

Meanwhile, the percentage of these bugs that are exploited in the wild remains relatively consistent. About 1.4 percent (1,363) of the CVEs published this year have been added to VulnCheck’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog.

“But obviously, as the number of CVEs grows, [1 percent] of 1,000 is a lot different than [1 percent] of 100,000,” Bressers said.

Plus, as other security researchers have documented, the window between the public release of a security patch and attackers developing working exploits – often by reverse engineering the patch while end users are still applying the fix – is rapidly shrinking. This is also thanks to AI.

From CVE to KEV

From January to June, 88 percent of the exploitation observed by CrowdStrike using public proof-of-concept (PoC) code occurred within 48 hours of the code's release. The security firm said China-linked groups such as Vault Panda and Genesis Panda moved even faster, launching attacks within 24 hours of disclosure.

Similarly, VulnCheck found the median time from CVE publication to exploitation falling from 120 days in 2025 to 80 days during the first half of 2026. This window has closed even further during the second half of the year, which also seems to coincide with the AI-induced vulnpocalypse.

“It’s often just hours,” Bressers said, noting 14 make-me-root vulnerabilities that VulnCheck disclosed on Friday in Copeland refrigeration controllers. Two are under active exploitation. These are the devices that Iranian hackers abused to spoil food and spark fires in supermarkets across Europe.

“We published those CVEs, and literally minutes later, we were seeing hits on our honey pots,” Bressers said about the Copeland device vulnerabilities. “We’ve hit a point where with anything that looks interesting, someone is taking that information and seeing what they can do with it. Is it AI driven? Probably. It'd be hard to say it's not, because we've seen it really ramp up recently.”

This influx of software bugs requires a sea change in how the entire industry approaches vulnerability disclosure and patching.

“We don't have a security problem anymore,” Bressers said. “We have a data problem now. Instead of obsessing over vulnerabilities, we need to start looking at things like heat maps for infrastructure, and figure out the vulnerabilities that actually affect you. The CISA BOD helps with that.”

What to prioritize in a patchpocalypse

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) in June issued a cybersecurity directive that replaces flat-deadline vulnerability management policies. Instead of prioritizing patching based solely on CVSS severity scores, the directive instructs organizations to prioritize based on specific risk criteria, including whether the asset is internet-exposed, under active exploitation, and whether an attacker can automate the exploit.

“It's telling people to figure out the vulnerabilities that actually affect you, and then put those at the top of the list, instead of just saying we're going to fix all the criticals,” Bressers said.

AI-generated vulnerability disclosures also create huge headaches for open source software developers and maintainers, which Bressers describes as a security problem “super close to my heart.”

“You've got individual developers that are drowning in vulnerability reports,” he said. “You have foundations being crushed by AI agents scraping their data or downloading their packages, millions of times a day, and it's straining the seams absolutely everywhere you look. The one thing I can say with certainty is: The way we currently do things has to change, and it's going to have to change fairly soon.”

Different open source projects have taken different approaches to solving this issue. The Eclipse Foundation, which houses the Open VSX Registry, in April launched a “managed tier” for enterprise customers and other organizations running Open VSX at scale.

Instead of using the free, open source version, the managed version guarantees a 99.95 percent uptime SLA backed by service credits. Its customers include AWS, IBM, Google, Cursor, and Windsurf. This paid option means commercial users who rely on the registry help fund its ongoing maintenance - and their own platforms’ security and performance.

Meanwhile, curl’s maintainer, Daniel Stenberg, citing an “avalanche of vulnerability reports," updated its bug reporting rules last month. As of October 26, all low- and medium-severity reports go directly into the public GitHub repository, with only the high- and critical-flaws receiving private handling.

Stenberg already shuttered curl's bug bounty program this year as AI-generated submissions piled work onto its security team.

“A lot more needs to happen, and I think it is going to be a challenge to enact some of this change,” Bressers said. “When a package registry drastically changes something, people start freaking out, and the world is going to end, and people on LinkedIn are complaining - a lot of people are hesitant. No one wants to be the first to jump into the alligator-filled pool. That's one of our challenges.”®

articles.title: Meatbags suck at spotting lying LLMs, so let AI narc on itself
articles.text:
The internet is full of schlock, from biased news and dubious hot takes to false factoids. LogicLens aims to separate fact from fiction using the very same technology behind some of that slop: AI.

It’s a simple premise, really: LogicLens, which lives in Chrome as a browser extension, or on iOS in the form of a mobile app called Receipts, combs through articles, social media posts, and other content to check it not only for factual inaccuracies, but also for bad reasoning. LogicLens and Receipts claim to identify logical fallacies, flag reports that misrepresent information, detect content that attempts to polarize an issue, and the like.

It also cites sources, so if, for example, you need to call someone out on their BS, you’ll have ammunition. Or, if you’re trying to fact-check something before sharing it, you can get a more accurate view of the situation, and maybe post something else instead.

Using the Chrome extension is as simple as clicking on its icon in the list of extensions in the browser. On iOS, the Receipts app is found as a share option. Once it starts, LogicLens scans an article, post, video, etc. to find potential issues of factual or logical inconsistency and flags them for review.

If the facts of the matter turn out to contradict your worldview, LogicLens’ creators say they’re not trying to be partisan - you may just not be as informed as you need to be, which hopefully their tool will assist with.

“We're not trying to be the referee of truth,” the company’s about page states. “Instead, LogicLens helps uncover the context, so you can decide for yourself without the spin."

Of course, AI is increasingly used for online analysis and content review, and LogicLens is no exception. LogicLens doesn't identify the AI models powering its service in its publicly available documentation, but AI is definitely the backbone of the system.

According to LogicLens, it's using an AI system that's “Research-backed and custom designed to outperform general models like ChatGPT & even trained experts.” We’ll leave that up to anyone willing to give the tool a spin to decide, but one thing’s for certain: The world needs something.

Large language models and image generation tools are increasingly being used to generate internet content slop, and not all of it is as harmless as poorly made commercials for drop-shipped garbage: Some of it is being used to craft very convincing misinformation.

A 2024 study found that AI-generated misinformation was even more convincing than stuff crafted by humans - and that was two years ago. Just think how much worse it’s likely become since then.

To make matters worse, concerns have been raised about critical thinking skills being on the decline, potentially making it harder for people to identify falsehoods on the internet. AI users are reportedly less likely to admit they don’t know something, even though use of AI has been found in studies to lessen brain activity, leading to poorer retention of facts and worse performance on tests.

Is using more AI the solution to the problem? In an ideal world, we’d all just put the computers down and go touch grass, but we’re not in an ideal world: We’re living in the age of AI.

LogicLens is free but requires sign-up and restricts nonpaying users to 15 analyses a day and 100 over the course of a month. A $4.99 monthly subscription removes those analysis caps. ®

articles.title: In elephants, the resilience of communities has its limits
articles.text:
Elephants live in some of the most complex and resilient societies in the animal kingdom. Individuals die or move away, calves grow up, and newcomers join, but the local communities as a whole usually hold together. Long-term studies of African savanna elephants have shown that, even after poaching or other spikes in deaths, survivors tend to rebuild their lost connections over time. But a new study suggests that resilience may not keep the community intact when steady losses accumulate over time.

Anastasia Madsen, a behavioral ecologist at the University of California, San Diego, and her colleagues analyzed 12 years of observations of wild Asian elephants in Sri Lanka. They found that, once losses began to outpace newcomers, the elephants’ society didn’t just get smaller. It fractured.

Accidental savanna

Udawalawe National Park in southern Sri Lanka was created in the 1970s around a reservoir on one of the country's four major rivers. “Before that, it was basically a tropical deciduous forest,” said Shermin de Silva, an ecologist at UC San Diego and senior author of the study (de Silva started the Udawalawe Elephant Research Project in 2006).

articles.title: Microsoft's massive M365 outage stretches past 27 hours as its fixes keep failing
articles.text:
In Australia, they’re calling it the “Microsoft long weekend” – an outage so pervasive it’s just about made Friday a write-off at organizations which rely on Redmond’s online services, especially Exchange Online.

As The Register reported yesterday, the outage started on Thursday at around 18:00 UTC and saw Microsoft 365 users unable to access email, attend Teams meetings, use cloud PCs, consult Copilot, or enjoy full access to another 15 hosted services.

The software giant says the outage impacts Microsoft 365 services “that interact with Exchange Online and email services.” Services that don’t need Exchange Online remain functional.

The software giant initially blamed the outage on a mysterious “problem that's causing servers to fail automated health checks and become unavailable.”

Microsoft thought it found a fix but quickly admitted “Actions taken thus far have not provided the anticipated relief.”

In the hours since, the situation has not improved markedly, and Microsoft is still struggling to restore service.

It has also changed the language it uses when discussing the possibility that a cyberattack is the reason for the outage.

As of 04:11 UTC, the company said it could find “no indication this is the result of malicious activity.” An update time-stamped 05:46 UTC stated “As of now, we are not aware of any malicious activity that is causing this incident.”

Microsoft’s status page includes only the company’s most recent update, but its RSS feed preserves each missive. That feed tells a tale of woe that we have distilled into lowlights and present in chronological order:

  • We’re applying infrastructure capacity improvements where possible in an effort to help support traffic in regions coming online;

  • We’ve monitored the status of the changes applied to improve serviceability and confirmed that change is not taking as expected;

  • We’re reviewing traffic flows and affected infrastructure to identify opportunities to optimize routing. This includes verifying the reasons for service failures so we can develop specific actions to improve stability;

  • We’re identifying alternate workstreams that can be applied to increase capacity in the face of sustained traffic management imbalances;

  • We're observing partial recovery across regions in which we've applied these adjustments; however, these actions aren't resulting in sustained recovery;

  • Current actions we are taking include scaling up virtual machines to increase capacity and reduce load. However, we are encountering issues with the machines being stuck in a bad state, preventing our changes from syncing as expected.

Microsoft’s latest status update doesn’t suggest this will be over any time soon.

“We’re continuing to pursue multiple workstreams to pinpoint the underlying cause of the traffic influx and advance the recoverability of the backend servers,” Microsoft wrote. “We’re taking a measured approach to identify and repair affected infrastructure to improve the ability to confirm the developed changes were applied. We’re tracking the results of this approach to verify the servers are showing the anticipated recovery and performance intended.”

Hopefully, Australia and other countries in nearby time zones won’t be the only ones to get an unscheduled long weekend. ®

Updated to add at 2144 UTC
Redmond still claims that the situation is in the process of stabilizing with no estimate for when everything might get back to normal. "As infrastructure stabilizes, we're still draining queued messages and rebalancing traffic, so customers may see improved sign-in/access while delivery and processing continue to catch up," it writes on its status page. "We do not have an ETA for full recovery yet. Service access can recover before mail flow fully normalizes." The company issued its latest status update at 2002 UTC and promises another update by Saturday at 0000 UTC.

Updated to add at 1300 UTC
Microsoft says it's seeing continued recovery progress across affected regions, with "broader improvements now observed in North America and sustained improvements across much of Europe. We're also seeing encouraging recovery signals in Asia Pacific, although some users may continue to experience intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery as mitigation progresses across the remaining affected infrastructure."

Updated to add at 1200 UTC
The latest status update at 12:00 PM UTC admits users are still "unable to connect to multiple Microsoft 365 services."

articles.title: Design, develop & deploy: Sarvam signs 5-year MoU with MoD to build AI for Army, Navy, IAF
articles.text:
New Delhi: Bengaluru-based AI company Sarvam has signed a five-year memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Headquarters Integrated Defence Staff (HQ IDS), Ministry of Defence, setting up an umbrella framework for artificial intelligence projects across the Indian Army, Navy and Air Force.
HQ IDS announced the MoU on 26 October, and the company made it public Tuesday. In a post on X, the defence ministry said the two sides would collaborate “on AI applications, research, knowledge management, training and decision-support” across the three services.
HQ IDS was set up in 2001 following the recommendations of the Kargil Review Committee to coordinate planning and operations among the three services. The framework extends to the joint, tri-service and integrated organisations under it.
Under the pact, Sarvam will design, develop and deploy AI applications for the operational, training and decision-support requirements of the services and provide follow-on technical support, while HQ IDS will facilitate the engagement.
A significant step towards strengthening sovereign AI capabilities for India’s Defence Forces.
HQ Integrated Defence Staff and Sarvam #AI have signed a Memorandum of Understanding to collaborate on AI applications, research, knowledge management, training and decision-support… pic.twitter.com/GLKYWUDZMu
— HQ Integrated Def Staff (@HQ_IDS_India) October 26, 2026
According to the company, the services and joint organisations will get access to the same foundation models, agentic infrastructure, and geospatial and perception systems, so that doctrine and lessons from one service’s projects can feed into the next.
The focus areas are decision support, target acquisition and data fusion across the “sensor-to-shooter loop”—the chain from detecting a target to engaging it—with human oversight retained on operational decisions.
Sarvam said the AI layer would be built in India and deployed on sovereign infrastructure. Projects under the MoU include an “AI fabric” that connects the elements of India’s defence capabilities.
“Sarvam exists to build AI in India, for India,” said Pratyush Kumar, co-founder, Sarvam. He described working with the three services as “an honour and a privilege”, and thanked HQ IDS for its trust.
Neither side disclosed the financial terms, the number of projects or a timeline for deployment.
The work will be carried out by Chanakya, which Sarvam describes as its firewalled division for national security and defence. Sarvam announced Chanakya on 29 March this year, saying the team would work on on-premise deployments in air-gapped setups, multimodal data ingestion and agent-based workflows. Air-gapped systems are cut off from the internet, a requirement for classified military networks.
Chanakya will use Sarvam’s AI stack, including Sarvam 105B, a foundation model the company open-sourced in February. The model uses a Mixture-of-Experts architecture, in which only 10.3 billion of its 105 billion parameters are active at a time. It was launched at the India AI Impact Summit in New Delhi along with a 30-billion-parameter model, with support for 22 Indian languages.
The MoU builds on Sarvam’s work with a military training institution.
On 18 August, the Defence Services Staff College (DSSC), Wellington, launched DRONA 2.0, a generative AI platform for training, research and strategic studies that runs on Sarvam 105B along with open-source models.
DRONA, short for DSSC Resource Optimising Neural AI, was first launched on the college’s network on 16 June, 2025.
On 18 August, Lt Gen Manish Erry, Commandant, DSSC, launched the upgraded version in the presence of Sarvam co-founder Vivek Raghavan, and the two sides signed an MoU for further development of the platform and other AI applications. The system is hosted on a GPU server within the college’s secure network and was certified by HQ IDS and the Defence Cyber Agency after security audits.
Founded in 2023 by Raghavan and Kumar, Sarvam was selected in 2025 to build India’s sovereign AI model under the IndiaAI Mission. In June, it raised $234 million in the first close of its $300 million Series B round at a post-money valuation of $1.5 billion, with HCLTech investing $150 million as lead strategic investor. In August, it raised another $74 million from Nvidia, Activate, Glade Brook Capital and Gaja Capital to complete the round.
The company linked the latest agreement to the government’s push for ‘Atmanirbharta’ in defence and the indigenisation of defence equipment, which it said now extends to AI. The ministry’s work on military AI predates the pact: a 2019 executive order created the Defence AI Council and the Defence AI Project Agency, and an AI roadmap identifying 70 projects was drawn up for defence public sector undertakings.
Private firms have since moved into the space. According to startup data platform Inc42, 89 percent of Indian defence tech startups report integrating AI into their offerings, as demand rises for autonomous systems, surveillance and communications built in the country.
(Edited by Amrtansh Arora)

articles.title: Issuance of Rs 56.8 crore tender by Bharat Dynamics Ltd to its former CMD’s company under scanner
articles.text:
New Delhi: A Rs 56.8 crore tender issued by Bharat Dynamics Ltd (BDL) in May for the supply of optical sights to a company run by its former chairman and managing director has brought the defence public sector undertaking under scrutiny over potential conflict-of-interest concerns.
The controversy follows a report by The Indian Express that the Hyderabad-based defence PSU, citing “urgency”, issued a single tender for the optical sights to Aindri Defence Advisory Private Limited, a company set up by former BDL CMD Commodore Siddharth Mishra (Retd) and his wife after his retirement. His wife holds 95 percent stake in the company.
Mishra headed BDL from March 2019 to March 2023. He is currently serving as a member of the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT).
The tender covers the supply of 300 optical sights, with delivery required within seven months of the completion of acceptance and validation tests of five sample units supplied by the company.
Sources in the defence establishment told ThePrint that Aindri has supplied five sample units, all of which have cleared technical inspection by BDL. The financial evaluation of the company’s bid is underway, and no contract has been signed yet, they added.
Sources said due process had been followed in issuing the tender but declined to elaborate on the urgency cited to justify the single-tender route.
The delay in finalising the contract has also raised questions about the urgency cited for the procurement, given that the tender was issued in May and the financial evaluation remains underway.
An open tender allows multiple vendors to compete, potentially helping the procuring organisation secure more competitive prices. In urgent cases, however, procurement rules permit a restricted or single-tender process, subject to the applicable rules and approval requirements.
The circumstances surrounding the procurement, including the justification for urgency and the decision to invite only one company, are therefore key.
Sources explained that there is no general prohibition on former public-sector executives setting up businesses in the same sector after retirement. However, the fact that the company is linked to a former head of the procuring PSU raises questions about safeguards against actual or perceived conflicts of interest.
(Edited by Viny Mishra)

articles.title: 8 launch pads, 32 preparation zones: Satellite images confirm Russia built new drone base in 6 weeks
articles.text:
New Delhi: News agency Reuters confirmed Thursday the assessment by Telegram OSINT channels that Russia completed construction of a major new attack drone facility in approximately six weeks.
The rapid construction comes as Russia expands deployment of jet-powered strike drones capable of reaching speeds of 600 km/h, posing fresh challenges to Ukrainian air defences.
Planet Labs imagery from 31 August, 2026 showed an undeveloped field near Millerovo in Russia’s Rostov region. Groundwork began the following day, with construction captured by the Copernicus Sentinel-2 and commercial satellites.
By 11 October, Planet Labs imagery showed launch pads and buildings taking shape, while high-resolution Airbus and Planet Labs images from 12-14 October confirmed that the facility was nearing completion, with launch rails being installed.
The 0.9-sq km facility features eight launch pads and 32 preparation zones.
High-resolution imagery shows that physical launch rails have been erected on two pads, while guidance tracks are being installed at two others. The preparation zones would allow launch crews to fuel, programme and equip drones before deployment.
According to Ukrainian OSINT analysts, the facility’s layout closely mirrors that of an existing Russian jet-powered strike drone installation in Tsymbulova, in the Oryol region. The new site is just 3.5 km from Millerovo airbase, placing it within the air-defence coverage associated with the base, according to private threat intelligence firm DroneSec.
DroneSec analyst Mike Monnik told Reuters that the facility could support Russia’s deployment of Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet-powered drones as part of a network of more than 11 strike locations across the country.
He warned that the speed of construction, combined with faster drones and gaps in NATO-provided counter-drone capabilities, could create significant vulnerabilities for Ukraine.
“The speed of construction demonstrates just how easily Russia can quickly deploy its already established offensive capabilities,” Monnik told Reuters. He added that the facility could launch more than 100 jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) a day, although actual deployments would generally occur in smaller waves.
Ukrainian forces have claimed that Russian deployments of jet-powered strike drones have reportedly increased six-fold over the past three months. Kyiv and surrounding areas have been among the principal targets as Moscow increasingly relies on jet-propelled systems to conduct strikes against Ukrainian territory.
Their higher speeds also complicate interception. Although relatively inexpensive interceptors costing less than $2,000 have been used against Geran-3 and Geran-4 drones, the long-term effectiveness of such systems remains uncertain.
The expansion of Russia’s drone capabilities comes amid a wider dispute over attacks on energy infrastructure and the role of US military assistance to Ukraine.
US President Donald Trump has urged Kyiv to halt strikes on Russian energy infrastructure ahead of a US-Russia diesel agreement, amid wider conflicts in West Asia.
In an interview with Financial Times published Wednesday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Ukraine had refrained from conducting deep strikes against Russian energy targets for three days, but Russian attacks on Ukrainian civilian and energy infrastructure continued to intensify. He said Kyiv would continue targeting Russian oil facilities, claiming that Ukrainian strikes had taken between 40 and 50 percent of Russia’s capacity offline.
Zelenskyy also said he would agree to stop attacks on Russian energy infrastructure in exchange for American Patriot air-defence interceptors, describing them as the “minimum” Ukraine would require. However, he said the response instead involved degraded Starlink services.
Ukraine separately reported a one-day restriction on SpaceX’s Starshield service which it said affected drone interceptions and strikes. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said that the restrictions were imposed by US Central Command.
Ashwin Shekhar is an alum of ThePrint School of Journalism, currently interning with ThePrint.
(Edited by Amrtansh Arora)
